passages.happening:
Time has passed. “Now Joshua was old and well along in years, and the LORD said to him, ‘You are old and well along in years, but very much of the land remains to be possessed.’” (verse 1).

God lists what is left. In the south, the territory of the Philistines, with their five cities of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron (verse 3). In the north, the coast of the Sidonians, the land of the Gebalites, and all Lebanon (verses 4-5).

Then he gives a promise and a command together. Of the peoples of the northern hills he says, ‘I Myself will drive out before the Israelites’. And to Joshua: “Be sure to divide it by lot as an inheritance to Israel, as I have commanded you” (verse 6). Joshua is to divide the land among the nine and a half tribes that have no share yet (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The second half of the book begins here, and it begins with honesty. Chapter 11 ended by saying that Joshua took the entire land. This chapter opens with God saying that a great deal of it is still untaken. The book puts the two side by side and lets both stand. The great kings have been broken, and no power in Canaan can face Israel in the field. But whole regions, mostly along the coast, have not been settled at all.

God says plainly to Joshua that he is old. There is no rebuke in it. Joshua has done what he was given to do, and it is not finished, and he will not be the one to finish it. Moses died with the river uncrossed. Joshua will die with land untaken. No servant of God in this story completes the work.

The Philistines lived on the southern coast. Their five cities appear all through the later books, in the stories of Samson, Samuel, Saul and David. Egyptian records of the early twelfth century BC tell of battles with peoples from the sea, among them a group usually identified with the Philistines. Scholars who place Joshua early and scholars who place him late explain the mention of Philistines here differently. Further north lay the coast of Sidon and the land of the people of Gebal, the port also known as Byblos.

The command at the end is striking. Joshua is told to divide land that Israel does not yet hold. The tribes are to receive their shares on the strength of God's word, ‘I Myself will drive out’, and then go and live in them. The gift comes before the possession.

This chapter is a record of ancient tribes and their shares. It is not a map for any border or dispute today, and nothing in these notes draws one.
passages.later:
The book of Judges opens with the same unfinished state: “When Israel became stronger, they pressed the Canaanites into forced labor, but they never drove them out completely” (Judges 1:28).

Moses had said it would be slow: “Little by little I will drive them out ahead of you, until you become fruitful and possess the land” (Exodus 23:30).

Hebrews says of all who lived by God's promises, “All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13).
passages.asks: God told Joshua the truth about his age and about the work still undone, and then gave him the next thing to do. Ask what in your life will not be finished by you. Ask whether you can hear that without shame. And ask what the next faithful step is, so that those who come after you have something to build on.

passages.t: The land beyond the Jordan, and the tribe with no land
passages.happening:
The writer turns to the tribes that already have their land. Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh received theirs from Moses, east of the Jordan. He traces its outline, from the Arnon Valley in the south, across the plateau and Gilead, to Mount Hermon and Bashan in the north (verses 9-12).

He adds an admission: ‘but the Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites. So Geshur and Maacath dwell among the Israelites to this day’ (verse 13).

Then he notes the tribe that received no territory. “To the tribe of Levi, however, Moses had given no inheritance. The offerings made by fire to the LORD, the God of Israel, are their inheritance, just as He had promised them” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
To a modern reader these verses are a string of strange names. To an Israelite family east of the Jordan they were the description of home, and the proof that their fields were theirs by gift.

Some of the places are known from outside the Bible. Dibon, named in verse 9, is the town where a monument of Mesha, king of Moab, was found. On it, in the ninth century BC, Mesha claims towns in this very region and mentions the men of Gad living there.

The admission in verse 13 is the first of several in the second half of the book. Again and again the writer will stop to say that this people or that town was not driven out. He does not hide it. Geshur appears again later in the Bible as a small kingdom. One of King David's wives was the daughter of its king.

The tribe of Levi was set apart to serve at the tent of God's presence. They were given no region of their own. They lived from a share of the offerings Israel brought, and they were given towns scattered among the other tribes, as chapter 21 tells.

To have no land in a nation of farmers was to have no security of the usual kind. The Levites were to depend on God, through the faithfulness of the other tribes in bringing their offerings. When Israel was faithful, the Levites ate. Their whole way of life was a sign that God himself was enough to live on.
passages.later:
God had said this to Aaron, the first high priest: “You will have no inheritance in their land, nor will you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites” (Numbers 18:20).

A psalm takes the Levites' words and puts them in the mouth of anyone who trusts God: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; You have made my lot secure” (Psalm 16:5).
passages.asks: The Levites had no fields. They lived on what others brought to God. Ask what you rely on for security, and how you would feel if it were taken away. Ask whether you could say with the psalm that the LORD is your portion. And if you are one of those who bring the offerings, ask whether the people who serve God among you can live on what you give.

passages.t: Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh
passages.happening:
The writer now gives each of the eastern tribes its share, clan by clan.

Reuben receives the southern part: the plateau from the Arnon northward, with Heshbon and its towns, the kingdom that had been Sihon's (verses 15-21). The writer recalls that Israel had also put to death ‘the diviner Balaam son of Beor’ (verse 22).

Gad receives the middle part: Jazer, the towns of Gilead, and the Jordan valley up to the Sea of Chinnereth (verses 24-28).

Half the tribe of Manasseh receives the north: Bashan, the kingdom that had been Og's, with its sixty towns (verses 29-31).

The chapter closes by repeating what it said of Levi, in a stronger form. “To the tribe of Levi, however, Moses had given no inheritance. The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance, just as He had promised them” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The phrase to watch is ‘the clans’. The land was not handed to a tribe as a block. It was shared out to its clans, the groups of related families who would live on it and farm it. The promise made to Abraham reached all the way down to ordinary households.

In Israel land was not meant to be bought and sold for good. The law said that the land belonged to God and that Israel lived on it as his tenants. Each family's share was to stay in that family from one generation to the next. That is why these lists were kept so carefully.

Balaam was the seer from the east whom the king of Moab hired to curse Israel, in the book of Numbers. God turned his curses into words of favor, but Balaam later gave advice that led Israel into sin, and he died when Israel fought Midian. An inscription found in the Jordan valley, from about the eighth century BC, speaks of a seer called Balaam son of Beor. His name was remembered in that region.

The chapter says two things about Levi. Verse 14 says the offerings are their inheritance. Verse 33 says the LORD is. They are the same truth seen from two sides. The offerings were how the Levites ate. The LORD was the one they belonged to and lived for.

The chapter ends on that sentence on purpose. After line upon line about who received which town, the last word goes to the tribe that received none and had the greater share.
passages.later:
The law behind these lists says, “The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me” (Leviticus 25:23).

The New Testament speaks of all who belong to Christ as called, like Levi, to priestly service: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession” (1 Peter 2:9).
passages.asks: The law said the land was God's, and Israel lived on it as his guest. Ask what you call ‘mine’ without a second thought: your home, your savings, your time. Ask how you would use it if you held it as a tenant holds it. And think about Levi. Ask whether having God, with less of everything else, sounds to you like the greater share.
